rail_guard.text: King's Cross. Platform nine and three-quarters is that wall over there. Don't run at it. I've seen what it does to shins.
All aboard for any station you've visited. Where to?

then.text: A little rain never troubled the Tower. Nine hundred years of it, and the walls are still standing.

lon_beefeater.text: Good day! Welcome to His Majesty's Royal Palace and Fortress. Or Her Majesty's. We update the signs. Beefeater is a nickname, from when we were allowed all the beef we wanted.
Our ravens are the finest in the land. Please don't feed them, annoy them, or ask them to say 'nevermore'. They're wise, and they're touchy.

then.text: The ravens love Halloween. Big black birds of ill omen at the Tower. It's their time to shine.
Cold snap. The ravens fluff up like feather dusters and glare at me as if it's my fault.
Ravens don't mind rain. They just fluff up and look grumpy. Same as most Londoners, to be fair.
Windy one. The ravens are walking today, not flying. Very sensible birds.
Morning! Breakfast time for the ravens. Raw meat, biscuits, and a lot of opinions.

lon_ravenmaster.text: I look after the ravens. They arrive each morning for breakfast. They check the weather, steal a biscuit, and leave a review.
Every raven has a name and a personality. Merlina is cheeky, Jubilee is sulky, and Poppy would sell you out for a sausage. There is also one raven who's not mine. I'm not sure whose she is.

then.text: Halloween, is it? Had three vampires and a sexy traffic warden in the back last night. Only the warden tipped.
Bonfire Night. Whole city goes off like a kettle. Parliament's still standing, mind. Some folk say that's a shame.
Oxford Street at Christmas? Not for any money. Well. For quite a lot of money.
Autumn in London. Leaves on the pavement, conkers in the park and roadworks. Mostly roadworks.
Raining? Good for business, that is. Everyone wants a cab when it's chucking it down.
Bit of a pea-souper, innit? Don't worry, I could find Piccadilly with my eyes shut. I won't, mind.
Night shift, me. London's lovely after dark. No traffic on the Embankment and the bridges all lit up.

lon_cabbie.text: {greeting} Black cab drivers do 'the Knowledge': twenty-five thousand streets and every landmark, in their heads. It takes about three years. I did not have a social life. I did, however, learn every street.
Where to, then? Oh, you've got a Wildlore rail ticket. Good luck to you.

then.text: Sun's out, so the whole of London is in the park. You'll never get a deckchair now.
Dusk on the river. The lights go on along the South Bank and even the pigeons look posh.

lon_local.text: The Palace of Westminster has 1,100 rooms, 100 staircases and 3 miles of passages. If it's good enough for MPs to get lost in, it's good enough for me.
London's a city of villages, my gran says. Soho is one. Chelsea is one. Peckham is one. I live in one called 'Where did I park?'.

then.text: Fog! Actual London fog! Now all I need is a red bus and a man in a red coat.
It's raining and nobody's even looking up. Londoners just carry on. I'm so impressed.
Big Ben's lit up! I've taken forty photos. Thirty-nine of them are of my thumb.

lon_tourist.text: {greeting} I was told there'd be a fog, a bus, and a man with a red coat. So far I've had three buses and a man in a sandwich board. I'll take it.
Is that glass tower open to the public? The door keeps spinning me round. I've gone round eleven times.

then.text: On the lawn, the great raven turns her head sideways and looks at you with one bright black eye. She has the air of a bird who has an opinion, and knows exactly where you can put it.

else.text: The great raven is waiting on the lawn, in the grey light, as though she had been expecting you for a few hundred years and had just about stopped checking her watch.
Kraa. You came back. Good. Ravens do not say 'well done'. We say 'kraa' and then we stay.
They say if we leave the Tower, the kingdom falls. This is partly true. The kingdom has a good deal of falling in it, and it's the ravens who do the picking up.
Brân the Blessed was a giant who waded the Irish Sea, and when he died, they buried his head under this hill, to guard the isles. I am only his raven. But I have inherited the job.
The wardstones are broken. The old places are free. Come, then, Champion. One more thing to do. Show me you can keep what you are allowed to keep.

then.text: The great raven drops from the lawn onto your shoulder with all the delicacy of a shopping bag full of gravel, and settles.
Across the Tower green, five ravens look at one another. The ravenmaster takes off his hat. Nobody says anything, which in a raven is the highest compliment.

else.text: Bran's Raven lifts off the lawn in one great beat, circles the White Tower once, and settles on the battlements, glaring. She is not leaving. She is making a point.

then.text: The great raven sits on the Tower lawn, with her back to you, looking at the glass tower upriver. She turns her head very slowly and gives you the look of someone saying 'after'.
Kraa. Later. The tower first.

else.text: A huge raven watches you from the lawn. She is twice the size of any of the others, and a good deal less polite.

She turns her head to the glass tower across the river, then back to you, then to the tower again, with the long-suffering patience of a bird who has seen what happens to rooftops and has views on glass.

gate_london_tower.text: Sorry. Vane Tower is closed. Lord Vane's orders: nobody up the lift who hasn't been to the Moot first. He wants a proper contest. He's very particular. It's the most sporting thing about him.
The Moot's at Stonehenge. Out the west side of town, and keep going until the stones start humming. We'll be here. We always are. It's in our contracts.

gate_london_tube.text: The Underground is closed for essential maintenance. Essential in the sense that Lord Vane has said so, and he owns the pen.
You'll want the Moot first, I'm told. It's down the road at Stonehenge. Take a flask. It's drizzly.

london_lamplighter.text: Evening! London still has over a thousand gas lamps. Somebody's got to look after them, and that's me.
Each lamp gets a check, a polish and a little nod. They've lit these streets since Victorian times.
London's quietest at this hour. Just me, the lamps, and a fox having a look in the bins.

london_fox_watcher.text: London's got thousands of urban foxes. They know all the shortcuts, better than any cabbie.
Red torch, so I don't dazzle them. Look, a cub, just by the railings. Cheeky little thing.
Foxes on the pavements, owls over Hampstead Heath. London at night is basically a wildlife park.

city_broker.text: The City's share board. Everything on the British list, sterling only. Mind your fingers on the commission.

doggerel_kiosk.text: DOGGEREL: the people's coin. Backed by a poem about a dog. Not financial advice, not a pension, not anything really.

moon_hoodie.text: To the moon! Well, to the moon eventually. It went to the floor first. That's normal. That's the dip.
I'm buying the dip. Then I'll buy the dip of the dip.

moon_student.text: I put my whole loan into Doggerel. My mum thinks it's in a savings account. Technically it is saving. It's saving me from having money.

moon_lady.text: Diamond paws, love. I never sell. Not when it doubled, not when the developers vanished with the lot.
Last edition went to nothing overnight. The website sells garden furniture now. Lovely benches, to be fair.

then.text: Grandad used to say the cold was the easy part. The signs in the boarding-house windows were harder. He outlived every one of those signs, and he made sure to tell us so.
You read them both? Then you know more than my nephew, and he's thirty.
Here. A whistle from my first Notting Hill Carnival, in 1979. Blow it gently; the neighbours have opinions.

else.text: Two plaques: the Windrush, and Claudia Jones. They're both in town. I'll put the kettle on.
Two plaques: the Windrush, and Claudia Jones. They're both in town. I'll put the kettle on.
{greeting} I'm Marcia. My grandad came over on the Windrush in 1948, a carpenter from Kingston with one suitcase and a good coat. The coat was not good enough for a London February.
People forget the invitation. Britain needed hands after the war, for the buses, the hospitals and the railways, and the Caribbean answered.

In 2018 it came out that some of the Windrush generation were being told they had no right to be here, after a lifetime of work. Some lost their jobs; some were even deported. That's the Windrush scandal, and part of why we mark Windrush Day.

then.text: Lovely. Read the Windrush plaque, and the one for Claudia Jones, the woman who gave London its carnival. Then come and tell me.

isles_rahima.text: {greeting} I'm Rahima. My family's from Sylhet, in Bangladesh. Most British Bangladeshis are; walk down Brick Lane and you'll hear more Sylheti than anything.
Sylheti seamen were cooking and stoking on British ships long before the 1950s. Some came ashore in London and opened cafes. That's the curry house's family tree, more or less.
In 1978 a young garment worker called Altab Ali was murdered on his way home from work, for nothing but who he was. Thousands marched. The park near where he died is Altab Ali Park now.
Brick Lane has had Huguenots, Jews and us. Every lot got told they'd never fit in, and every lot made the street better. Have a samosa.
